title: Lesson 001 — Binary and Denary
source_note: Reading companion aligned to the current online lesson. Not a transcription or replacement of the four-page PDF.
learning_objectives: Explain why the unsigned 8-bit range is 0 to 255.
Write a simple print(...) statement in OCR Exam Reference Language.

vocabulary.meaning: A base-2 number system using only 0 and 1.
The base-10 number system used in everyday counting.

vocabulary.example: The rightmost 1 in 1001 is one bit.

vocabulary.meaning: The value represented by a digit's position.
vocabulary.example: The place values in eight-bit binary are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.

vocabulary.meaning: The highest-value bit in a binary number.
vocabulary.example: In eight-bit unsigned binary, the leftmost bit has place value 128.

blocks.text: Try all four retrieval questions before opening any model answers.

blocks.prompt: 1. Which two digits are used in binary?
2. How many bits make one byte?
blocks.answer: B — 8. A byte contains eight bits.

blocks.prompt: 4. Four independent switches can each be ON or OFF. How many combinations are possible? Explain your calculation.
blocks.answer: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations, because each extra switch doubles the possibilities.

blocks.text: Binary is base 2, so each bit is either 0 or 1. A bit with value 1 contributes its place value. A bit with value 0 contributes nothing.

blocks.caption: Eight-bit unsigned binary place values, from left to right.

blocks.heading: Convert binary 10011100 to denary
steps: Write the eight place values above the digits.

blocks.heading: Convert denary 154 to eight-bit binary
steps: Choose 2: remainder 0. Fill the other columns with 0.

blocks.text: Eight bits have 2⁸ = 256 possible patterns. As 00000000 represents zero, the unsigned values run from 0 through 255.
Digital circuits can distinguish two states reliably. Binary allows computers to store and process numbers, text, images and sound.

blocks.heading: Convert 11001010₂ to denary
steps: Line up 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 beneath the binary digits.

blocks.prompt: Convert 01101001₂ into denary. Show the place values.
Explain why the highest unsigned eight-bit value is 255 rather than 256.
blocks.answer: Eight bits give 2⁸ = 256 patterns, including zero, so the values range from 0 to 255.

blocks.prompt: Write a print(...) instruction to display the value of binary 1011.

blocks.text: Code First: complete the three mini-whiteboard prompts, then attempt the independent exam-style questions. Check answers only after trying each question.

blocks.prompt: Code First 1. Predict what print(8 + 2 + 1) displays.
Code First 2. Write a print(...) instruction for binary 1010.
Code First 3. Modify two lines to store and display binary 1001.
Q2. Convert 01101001₂ to denary. Show working.
Q3. Convert denary 154 to unsigned eight-bit binary.
Q4. Convert denary 191 to unsigned eight-bit binary.
Q5. A student says an unsigned byte can store 0 to 256. Explain why this is incorrect.
blocks.answer: Eight bits represent 256 different patterns, but the first pattern represents 0. The maximum is therefore 255, not 256.

blocks.prompt: Is 255 the largest unsigned number that can be stored in eight bits? Yes or no?
blocks.answer: Yes. Eight bits represent 256 values, from 0 to 255.

blocks.text: Reflect: Can you convert binary to denary and denary to binary? Which step would you like to practise again?

memory_aids.title: Double as you move left
memory_aids.text: Starting at 1 on the right, double each place value: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

memory_aids.title: 1 means include, 0 means leave out
memory_aids.text: To convert binary to denary, add only the place values below digits that are 1.

memory_aids.title: Remember the maximum
memory_aids.text: Eight bits give 256 combinations. Since counting starts at 0, the maximum is 256 − 1 = 255.

memory_aids.title: Work from the largest place value
memory_aids.text: For denary to binary, start at 128 and choose the largest place value that fits. Keep subtracting until the remainder is zero.
